newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says don't rush Chechnya negotiations.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says don't rush Chechnya negotiations.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, touching only briefly on one of the big problems facing Russia in his state of the nation speech, cautioned on Thursday against rushing negotiations with Chechnya.

"Talks are continuing. Step by step confidence is being restored. But it is easy to destroy it and for this reason it is dangerous to artificially speed up the negotiating process," Yeltsin said in his annual address to members of parliament.

His comments contrasted with suggestions by negotiators from both sides last Sunday that Russia and Chechnya might soon sign a formal peace declaration after their almost two-year conflict which ended last August.
Under the August peace deal, the two sides agreed to defer for five years a decision on Chechnya's political status, the issue at the root of their conflict.
Chechnya's separatist leaders still demand full independence but Moscow has ruled this out. The risk of further clashes remains, although both sides' leaders appear keen to avoid more violence.
"The main thing has been achieved -- peace in the Chechen Republic has been restored. This is an imperative condition for the solution of all acute problems," Yeltsin said.
"The Chechen crisis has taught us a lot. The bloodshed has been stopped with great difficulty. So that wounds could heal, so that emotions could give way to common sense we need time."

Yeltsin has publicly regretted his decision to send troops to Chechnya in December 1994. Tens of thousands of people died in the fighting that followed in the mainly Moslem region in Russia's north Caucasus.
